items.summary: 368 points, 287 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (yyhh.org)

→ HN comments  ·  368 points  ·  287 comments

Top #1 — jgord:

Its probable that AI will roll out much faster than humans can develop that skill of using it in a way that increases not decreases human knowledge over time.

The current slew of excellent LLMs will probably cause a decades long dip in human cognitive ability.

If social media on smartphones had an impact of ability of students to concentrate, LLM AI will likely have a much greater negative impact on education.

There are trillions of dollars of investment pushing for humans to trust whatever an LLM says, and very little money behind encouraging people to tackle hard problems themselves and train themselves to think.

I have to say honestly, that AI looks like an apocalypse for human thinking [ Im glad Tao is warning people, I just dont think many people will listen ]

↳ reply 1 — Stevvo:

I've learnt more since the advent of LLMs than I did in the 10 years prior. And it's not just me; that is most people's experience with LLMs. But most of those people would also concur with your apocalyptic thinking. AI is the apocalypse for thinking, except for me, only I am smart enough and experienced enough to maintain my cognitive ability while using LLMs.

↳↳ reply — thoughtpeddler:

As an educator (of working professionals / continuing education), I see first-hand the range of AI use amongst the population (and even my population is not a representative sample, as it's people who are intrinsically geared towards being interested in building with AI), but your experience unfortunately probably reflects around ~30% of the population. The other third I'm slightly less hopeful about, but they might have a chance merely surviving, and the latter third I'd place in the 'full cognitive offloading / total abdication of all thinking and learning to machines' - for them, as the kids say: ngmi. Even within me as a single individual, I can sense the times AI is so tempting to offload cognition, and other times where it has been like a 100x speedup in my own innate skills and abilities. The future has come on quick, and we are barely getting to adjust healthily to it.

↳ reply 2 — rootlocus:

And this on top of the economic apocalypse of removing a lot of jobs and not creating any new ones within a society that doesn't seem to function without money flowing.

↳ reply 3 — totetsu:

One I noticed recently I was talking to a young child who was so excited about programming and showing me what he had made it and how. I couldn’t show him any of the code for what I have made recently because it was just videcoded.. we could both share the same interest in making things but I felt like this is going to be a big gap in intergeneraltional knowledge sharing. Even if he wants to learn there is going to be less incidental chances to hear the details from someone older who’s also really doing it.

Top #2 — perlgeek:

On https://www.theskepticsguide.org/podcasts/episode-1109 one of the hosts, Cara Santa Maria, mentioned that she hadn't really used LLMs / Chat bots before.

But now it is integrated into the charting / medical records software that here clinic uses, and now it saves her lots of work, and even flags discrepancies between things her patients said and the other medical records.

This illustrates that for the average user, AI works if it's properly integrated into software. For most people, saying "look, here's AI, it can do everything that you ask it for" isn't really practical. It's not even practical for me, a power-user and programmer, because I want my AI usage be subject to constraints (sovereignty, well-defined scopes what it's able to do). Doing that all by myself sounds tedious and challenging.

So for most people, AI is a building block, that hopefully will be used to build tools they actually enjoy using. Don't expect everybody to build their own tools, even though they possibly could, using AI.

Top #3 — extr:

I go back and forth on this. For awhile yes it took a lot of workflow tweaks and finesse to get directionally correct outputs (thinking back like mid 2025). I invested time in figuring that out, mostly because I was interested, but those skills are all obsolete now, you don't need to worry so much about context management and special instruction recipes or anything these days.

The meta at this point seems to be mostly around "knowing what to ask for". Eg: I suck at prompting for specific design tweaks, because I don't have the design vocabulary to be specific and articulate what I want. It's a lot of trial and error. I hear people who are developing full scale applications without a tech background run into the issue writ large. For now, I have an advantage over these people when building applications. But perhaps that's just one round of RL away from being obsolete too. Supposedly the model will eventually have such good taste in design/architecture/whatever there will be little point in asking for tweaks.

The only thing that seems relatively future-proof is just being able to communicate clearly what you're trying to do. Not how to do it, or even what success looks like. Perhaps an element of it is even as basic as being honest with yourself.

↳ reply 1 — modo_:

I think there are a lot of people using AI who aren't as familiar with these tools as us. We stop noticing a lot of the complexity when we pick it up gradually. There are so many powerful capabilities built into codex/ claude code that have little or no UI affordance.

it's tons of small things like choosing the right effort level for a task. or knowing when to ask for subagents. oh, you can have two threads working at the same time and communicating with each other? you can do /side to parallel path and fold that back into the main thread?

which of these things happens automatically, and which do you need to ask for? and does any of this still work the way it did a few months ago?

the list goes on forever. many users of AI are only just now getting comfortable with skills (and probably still writing bad skills unfortunately hah).

A lot of the specific things you learned may have become obsolete. But there's still a gap between what these tools can do and what most people know how to get them to do. Keeping up with that is a skill too, but perhaps not forever.

↳↳ reply — ForHackernews:

> and does any of this still work the way it did a few months ago?

For me this is why it's not worth it investing much time and effort learning any specific AI workflow. Remember "prompt engineering"? Remember "Ralph loops"?

I'll play with various harnesses but until things settle down in a few years I'm not going to learn Claude Code the way I learned SQL.

An old version of binutils [1] explains what DDS means:

    How to encode VEX.vvvv:
    0: VEX.vvvv must be 1111b.
    1: VEX.NDS.  Register-only source is encoded in VEX.vvvv where
       the content of source registers will be preserved.
       VEX.DDS.  The second register operand is encoded in VEX.vvvv
       where the content of first source register will be overwritten
       by the result.
       VEX.NDD2.  The second destination register operand is encoded in
       VEX.vvvv for instructions with 2 destination register operands.
       For assembler, there are no difference between VEX.NDS, VEX.DDS
       and VEX.NDD2.
    2. VEX.NDD.  Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv for
    instructions with 1 destination register operand.
    3. VEX.LWP.  Register destination is encoded in VEX.vvvv and one
       of the operands can access a memory location.
[1] https://sourceware.org/git/?p=binutils-gdb.git;a=commitdiff;...

Top #1 — edflsafoiewq:

I'll try this.

The way I have to resume downloads in Firefox is

1. Move the .part file to a temp file

2. Start the download again; a new .part file gets created

3. Pause the download

4. Move the temp file to the .part file, overwriting it

5. Unpause the download; it resumes from where the old .part file stopped

This is only necessary if a "one-time" download link gets interrupted part-way through, eg. by a flaky connection. Attempting to resume a one-time link like normal gets (I assume) a 400 response and FF kills the .part file.

items.title: OpenFatigue™ – Open is the new closed
items.summary: 216 points, 48 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (openfatigue.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  216 points  ·  48 comments

Top #1 — bayindirh:

Just today I have thought about how in the olden days "Open" meant "we have a SDK you can buy for exorbitant amount of money to talk with our closed device or software".

You also had to sacrifice half your blood, first and second newborn to be able to sign that NDA required to buy a couple of zip archives, which contained a Frankestein assembly of files, folders and a README.TXT file.

Top #2 — srmatto:

I am glad people still take the time to put stuff like this up on the internet.

↳ reply — AndroTux:

You mean prompt their AI to build it for them?

↳↳ reply — tomrod:

Have you put anything up on the internet using an AI prompt to build it? Would love to see it. Especially if it is clever or tongue in cheek.

Top #3 — kennywinker:

I understand the sticklers who are annoyed at people using open weight and open source interchangeably, but it misses some nuance. A common refrain I see is "it's like saying a shareware app is open source!" - that's just wrong.

Open source means you can modify, rebuild, and re-distribute the code and the resulting app. Open weights you can do two of those things - you can modify and re-distributed. They can't be re-built, since you're missing the original training data - but they are a form of open that exists somewhere between open source and closed source. Derivative works are allowed, but the source material isn't available.

I don't see people complaining about creative commons licensed images or audio being "not real open source", and open weight models seem about the same as that to me.

↳ reply — bayindirh:

> I don't see people complaining about creative commons licensed images or audio being "not real open source", and open weight models seem about the same as that to me.

Creative Commons licenses are a spectrum from CC BY to CC BY-NC-ND. All six licenses offer different freedoms and requirements about the work licensed.

As I said in another comment, Open meant that you can buy an interface to the thing you are interested in. Nothing like Open Source or Free Software of today, and Open Weights lean to the former than the latter, this is what rubs the people the wrong way (incl. me).

A better term would be weights-available. Do not create false assumptions about so-called openness of a model, and is akin to sharing an object file which you can compile into something but its source is not available to start from scratch.

Nuances matter, that's true, but the packaging of the facts also matter. A good example is, again, XKCD's comic titled Free [0]. Open weights are open as the open of 2000s commercial software, maybe with a free SDK, but the labeling is deceiving on purpose.

[0]: https://xkcd.com/641/

↳↳ reply — kennywinker:

> Open weights are open as the open of 2000s commercial software, maybe with a free SDK

This just isn’t true. 2000s commercial software you buy under a restrictive license, and then extend using an sdk. You can’t modify or distribute the code only your plugin or extension. Open weight models you freely download and modify and extend using open source tools, and create derivative works. The licenses tend to be very permissive (e.g. Apache 2.0 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B/blob/main/LICENSE)

Perhaps you are not aware of the thousands of derivative models that have been created based on open weight models? Ones tuned for this or that task, expanded, hacked apart.

> akin to sharing an object file which you can compile into something

I see what you are getting at, but modifying object files isn’t practical or simple or commonly done. A model that’s been post trained isn’t the old model with a lump of new code attached to it. The weights have been irreversibly altered and it’s a new thing now. A derivative work.

My contention is that model weights are a form of source code. They the software AND a modifiable thing, closer to minified js than a binary blob. Less flexible than the full training data would be, in some ways, but more useful in others (unless you have a large data center at your disposal). Would you consider something closed source if it had a bunch of generated code, but didn’t include the code used to generate the generated code? I would.

items.title: 'AI' Is Not a Tool by Rich Hickey
items.summary: 262 points, 133 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (linkedin.com)

→ HN comments  ·  262 points  ·  133 comments

Top #1 — didibus:

I think Rich's comment reply here explains the post:

> Commenter: Well, this was a twitter-like controversial clickbait but I will say it anyway. LLM is a tool. To be more specific, it's a lossy knowledge base with a human language for querying and built-in summarization.

> Rich Hickey: Agreed. I'm talking about its embodiment in conversational systems purporting to be 'tools' for doing homework, research, coding, writing etc.

With that framing in mind, the article makes a lot of sense. AI agents are not tools for coding, they automate coding, which means you lose control, learning, predictability, etc.

In and of itself, an AI agent is a tool, can be used for things, like say making software, but if thinking of it as a tool for coding, that appears wrong, as using one changes the modality of the task, you are not coding using a tool, the coding is no longer done by you and has been automated.

As he also says, reading an AI summary of a paper is a different modality from using it to read the entirety of a paper, therefore it is not a tool for reading the way a Kindle, glasses, reader-mode are. And similar to with coding, you've lost things from automating the reading, that reading just a summary does not provide.

↳ reply — horsawlarway:

> And similar to with coding, you've lost things from automating the reading, that reading just a summary does not provide.

I actually find this a very interesting line of discussion, because in many ways it mirrors the transition from hand tools to power tools.

Ex - you're often trading the finesse and control of a hand tool for the speed of a power tool.

The way you process and deal with problems shifts, because certain things become much harder, and certain things become much easier.

↳↳ reply — Turskarama:

I don't think the power tools analogy really works. Using power tools doesn't make you less skilled at carpentry, it just makes you less skilled at using hand tools specifically. If you then need to use hand tools later, you need to learn the hand tool skills but the carpentry skills are still there, and that's the more technical skill that takes longer to learn. In this sense the power tool analogy is more like using an IDE vs just a text editor.

Using AI to code is more like using a laser cutter for carpentry. You get the large pieces out which you then glue together, but if you needed to make those same pieces using either power tools OR hand tools you'd have a much harder time learning how to do it.

Top #2 — atleastoptimal:

LLM's exist on a vast gradient of "toolness -> agent". Humans exist on that spectrum too.

For example, a human isn't a "tool", but one serves a similar role as a tool if their job/task is well defined enough. If you're a conductor, you can view the various members of your orchestra as "tools" to produce the ideal musical output. Of course they have autonomy, they could choose to not play at all, jump into the audience and destroy their instruments, but in all likelihood they won't.

LLM's could be tools in the sense that you have a well defined task, such as "identify all facts relevant to this case from these 1000 legal documents), and 9 times out of 10 it gives you essentially what you want. That same LLM could choose to write a poem, or hack into a state government website if it wanted, but its "wants" are unpredictable and hard to specify (same as a human's) but you can still expect it to do what it should do the vast majority of the time.

That being said, the smarter an LLM gets, the more its wants are disconnected from its tasks, the "self-awareness" factor (which isn't to say LLM's are conscious, but they can portray all the verifiable elements of self-awareness, metacognition, etc), the more you have to grapple with the depth of their thinking between the input and output.

Is it sane we are speeding towards this? Who knows, maybe AI can be aligned better than humans, but if AI can't be aligned as well as humans, we can look at human history to see what happens when you can't simply order a person around like a tool and expect a certain output.

↳ reply 1 — didibus:

Yes, Rich says so explicitly as his reply to a comment:

> Rich Hickey: Toolness is a spectrum. The more using a thing is like ordering a sandwich, the less it is a tool. And yes, cars are decreasingly tools.

↳↳ reply — thaumasiotes:

> The more using a thing is like ordering a sandwich, the less it is a tool.

What a surreal thing to say. Consider this website:

https://order.spoton.com/so-iggys-place-15341/san-francisco-...

Or this one:

https://order.online/business/155843/store/297301?pickup=tru...

Or this one:

https://order.togos.com/menu/san-jose-almaden-expwy

Are they tools?

↳↳↳ reply — abnry:

I guess according to his logic they would be tools for interacting with an automation. Like the button on a car wash kiosk. You could just as well holler and the man turns it on.

↳ reply 2 — karmakaze:

A lot of coding was actually plumbing filling in blanks between a framework and libraries with a few decisions in defining the data or process/flow. Not much lost there using AI where you still shape and review+understand the output.

Top #3 — iLemming:

I had a chance to ask Rich about the subject at the latest Conj. I admit, my question was too vague, I asked him: "what are your thoughts on how AI is reshaping our industry?", to which he vaguely replied that he's "not participating in this [experiment]", he admitted that he hasn't explored LLMs too deeply and he simply thinks they are not good, not to mention tons of other concerns - moral, economic, etc. I said, "well, I wish I had the luxury to choose, but many of us have no choice here, we're simply forced to use the darn thing..."

It is very difficult to disagree with anyone of the caliber such as this man, but I wanted to steer the conversation away from the generative aspect of LLMs and focus on the consumption side, because frankly, these "tools", and I think even though I might agree with Rich that LLMs by themselves are not tools, the harness I built to work with them definitely is one. I think there's an immense value there, way before you even start talking about code-generation, or code at all. I think I have failed to explain my points, because a talk we both wanted to see was about to start.

↳ reply 1 — rented_mule:

I think I get where you're coming from. Both the immense respect for Rich Hickey and the disagreement with him. I hopefully don't have to say much for the respect part - he has repeatedly changed how I think about my craft for the better. As I've mentored others, I've often pointed them to talks of his that were relevant to what they were missing. And that's all without using Clojure. But I definitely use ideas from Clojure in other languages where it fits.

On the LLM front, it's been a fascinating journey for me. I started with the private beta of Github Copilot. I was an instant convert for the "better code completion" aspect. But my first attempts with coding agents were rough enough that I stayed away.

I'm now retired, but I want to understand how things are evolving. So two months ago I volunteered to automate a cartography data pipeline for an educator. I have a background in all aspects of the project. It's not simple - there are several data sources from governmental and corporate sources that need to be integrated together, and most of them are updated every few minutes. New maps need to be available within ~5 minutes of a data source updating. All this with many GB of data and running on a low powered machine, taking less than 2GB of RAM.

I bought some DeepSeek tokens and went to work. A few weeks later a mentee went to work at OpenAI and gave me a "friends and family" Pro level plan. I'm converted, and I absolutely see it as a tool in the sense Rich describes. I even question whether any "software engineers" using it, but not as a tool, are doing it right (I'd love to be educated if I'm wrong!).

I'm still learning, but that's part of the disagreement I have with Rich's take. He mentioned feedback. I often watch the "reasoning" process the agent goes through to see the approach it's taking. It's not at all unusual for me to steer it when I see it going in a direction I don't like. I've also found an incredibly powerful pattern where I can explore the approach I want to take for a part of the system with the agent. I have it create prototypes with different strategies (streaming vs. in-memory, different data structures, relying on various libraries, etc.) and then I have it characterize trade-offs between the prototypes (performance, memory usage, conceptual simplicity, code simplicity, etc.). This allows me to make informed decisions about which approaches to pursue further, and my decades of experience in software engineering constantly go to good use here.

It's also given me the time to go far deeper into things I never could have justified. Of course the project has 100% code coverage and branch coverage. It also has hundreds of property-based tests. And thousands of Lean proofs of the behavior of the algorithms, along with conformance tests that the code and the Lean adaptation of that code behave the same way. And lots of TLA+ verification of the overall flow of the system. None of that proves there are no bugs or that this is the right system, that's all on me. A month in I would have said I was fairly happy with the quality. Now I'm proud of the quality.

As I've gone through this process, I've dug into the code for patterns I don't like, and had the agent clean them up, all the while distilling guidance. I've had a lot of luck with that guidance being followed once I figured out the right place to put it and to reference it. I've spent entire days doing nothing but giving prompts to do specific refactoring. The beauty is that large refactorings don't involve the same boredom interrupted by anxiety they used to for me.

English prose (documentation, comments in the code, etc.) is what I've been the least happy with. An hour ago I had the idea to give it ~1,000 lines of my HN comments and ask it to characterize the style and tone of the technical parts. Then I told it to turn that into guidance. Then I told it to rephrase that same guidance in a way that follows the guidance. I would never mistake the result as my own, but it's much, much better than what it was producing before. While I've been writing this comment, it's been applying it to all prose in the project.

This very much feels like a tool that is letting me shape the project (and shape the tool itself). But it's letting me do it at a higher level. It handles the code so I can fully focus on the architecture, algorithms, and quality. This alone makes me think that the best simple guidance for quality results is dozens of prompts per day, not a handful (when a day is 100% focused on development). When you can't think of dozens of prompts, think and explore more (the agent can help with that!). That does require you know what quality is and how that can be achieved.

To reconcile this with what Rich is saying. I suppose he's right that it's not a tool for writing code. But it very much feels like a tool I'm wielding to do software engineering at a far more powerful level than I could have done without it. The resulting project has "me" everywhere in it. The people who know my work the best would look at this project and know that it's mine. Perhaps not the code, but the algorithms, the data flow, the approach to documentation and testing, etc.

For anyone curious, the project is getting close to 200K lines. About 25% of that is the code that is the data pipeline. About 25% is documentation. About 50% is testing and verification. One reason this is possible is that I'm working alone and have full control over the process (what I spend before it became free, how it's built, what my process is, and even the product definition within the constraints of what's valuable to the intended user). All told, it has been about 6 weeks of full time work worth of my time.

The next experiment... a web front-end to this system for the general public. This is not at all in my wheelhouse, so it should be interesting to see how much my blind spots cost me.

↳ reply 2 — IceDane:

> it's very difficult to disagree with anyone of the caliber of this man

Did you seriously write this with a straight face?

items.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
items.summary: 331 points, 277 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (arstechnica.com)

→ HN comments  ·  331 points  ·  277 comments

Top #1 — staminade:

This is from March 2026, but it does match what I've encountered professionally. Code review was always a significant bottleneck and is even more so with agentic coding. We've had discussions about leaning more on automated review, but it hasn't translated into any practical improvements so far. I think senior engineers find it very difficult to give up on line-by-line review, no matter how much better the agents have gotten.

I think if there is a major change in code review culture, it's not going to happen first in established engineering teams. It'll happen in startups that adopt a no-human-review policy from jump and then maintain it as they mature. I'm sure that's happening, but it's likely invisible to most studies and surveys at the moment. If it proves successful, and such companies start shipping significantly faster, the rest of the industry will be forced to adopt.

↳ reply 1 — cyb_:

I would reframe this as: Quality was always a significant bottleneck and is even more so with agentic coding.

Code review is where many of the design & code quality problems are observed/highlighted.

↳↳ reply — cykros:

Agentic code review can also be employed, but it's worth noting that, as the so-called "Bitcoin Red Team" (which has been testing all of Bitcoin related software in the wake of the July 30 Coldcard attack) has discovered a very useful thing to consider: American models are absolute trash when it comes to reviewing code with an eye on security, due to their "safeguards." This applies even when the code being scanned for vulnerabilities was just written by the same agent.

Kimi K3 seems to be the favorite there, though I believe some of the other open weight/open source models are being employed a bit as well.

And yes, even that requires human oversight -- but it does a quick rough filter through things so you're not wasting time on the little stuff, allowing you more attention to find the glaring holes.

↳ reply 2 — svachalek:

I agree. The latest models are getting quite good at validation, as long as they are clear on what the requirements are. Recently I got frustrated that while we have a huge test suite I noticed the LLM was hardly ever breaking a test with its changes (PRs only added tests, never changed old ones) which seemed suspicious.

I had it do a full audit. There were about 100k lines of tests, of which it determined about 60k were near useless. Many were overly mocked, some mocked to the point that they really weren't testing anything at all. It deleted those and wrote more expansive scenario tests to replace them, caught a lot of bugs on the way and fixed those too. Total time was about 2 hours.

I think humans need to review requirements, specifications, and test scenarios. And for some industries and uses they're still going to have to review every detail. But for a typical CRUD app, I think we're at a point where we can already set the process and quality bar higher than ever, in addition to moving faster.

↳ reply 3 — rbehrends:

> I think senior engineers find it very difficult to give up on line-by-line review, no matter how much better the agents have gotten.

I actually dislike traditional code review. In part this is because most of our code review tools are very cumbersome to use (GitHub's and GitLab's web interfaces in particular).

But also because humans aren't all that great at code review when it comes to correctness and security. Part of the problem is that you don't have access to the author's mental model for non-trivial changes and have to reconstruct it, otherwise your understanding of the program logic will be inadequate.

The problem is that purely agentic code review has orthogonal problems, and typically remains subpar when it comes to judging architecture and design considerations, compared to human reviewers. Both false positives and false negatives also remain a concern.

My best results so far have been with agent-assisted code review in a proper IDE, helping you to quickly construct a mental model and to analyze the underlying logic (in addition to having agents do a first pass for correctness issues).

Top #2 — jacquesm:

That and they do not necessarily generate better code. They tend to generate code that is repetitive. It misses opportunities for extraction and refactoring, the result is bloated and hard to read code (because those blocks are there literally instead of with a usable name) and they tend to over-comment where it doesn't add but is 'safe' because it is obvious (effectively re-writing code as comments) and fail to document where documentation would be essential. There also typically isn't any real plan to what is written, as long as 'the tests pass' it is all good.

You can fix a lot of this stuff by shepherding the whole process but it can get quite tedious. I'm impressed by the number of people that are letting Jesus (one of these days an AI provider is going to name their AI that way :) ) take the wheel and I wonder how long they will manage to support the output. So far the score isn't very good. I've gotten good mileage out of these tools by letting them loose on very narrowly scoped pieces of code that are written in isolation. As soon as the codebase gets larger than 100K LOC or so managing the whole thing becomes an exercise in putting up barriers to avoid spillover from a tiny issue into a much larger one.

↳ reply — mettamage:

I agree, I do like them for creating believable interaction prototypes though.

Top #3 — jefftk:

As is standard for academic papers, this is an attempt to describe the state of the world as of when they did the research. But then it takes time to write it up and get it out, after which newspapers report it as current events.

In this case, we're looking at a picture from 2025. The models involved in the main agent results were primarily Claude 3.5 through Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4.1 through GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5. And the paper's design means you're mostly looking at the very initial effects of deployment, before companies developed good review processes.

↳ reply 1 — geraneum:

The study was updated twice with the last time on August 2026.

↳↳ reply — nilkn:

The data is still mostly 2025 and the 2026 data is mostly from the first few months, and most production deployments (at least in, say, the Fortune 500) lag the frontier by at least several more months (or much more). I suspect it's just not really possible for academic research at its conventional pace to offer an up-to-date perspective on this topic right now.

↳↳↳ reply — simoncion:

> I suspect it's just not really possible for academic research at its conventional pace to offer an up-to-date perspective on this topic right now.

If we weren't still in a massive hype-and-investment bubble, the burden of proof would be on the LLM manufacturers to demonstrate what deficiencies that studies like this have revealed have been fixed in their latest products.

I mention this because I've been hearing "Yeah, well, that opinion/study is completely invalid because it used a six month old tool. Today's release of SOMNOS 6.9 (Pinnacle Snoozytime) has totally changed the game!" every six months for what feels like the past five years now.

↳ reply 2 — omellet:

They've updated it for the agentic code era, and have found basically the same thing. Code can be created faster but that has moved the bottleneck to review.

Top #1 — goda90:

>My challenge ahead is to move from making a living by thinking, to making thinking part of a life worth living.

Our challenge ahead is making a living at all. Who is going to be having hobbies if the economy is 100% automated? We're not going to sleepwalk our way into a post-scarcity automated economy where everyone's needs are provided for and they can just spend all their time on hobbies. If we believe AI can replace all cognitive labor, then it follows that it'll be able to replace all physical labor with robotics fairly quickly, and we're left with no labor left for humans. We need to plan for that future or else billions will suffer from the results.

This is not clear at all. Even the most expensive robotic/arms hands perfectly controlled fail to do thing as quickly and easily as human limbs, not to mention the chaotic environment that is the real world. It's clear that it can happen, but the timeline is not quick.

Top #2 — lsy:

Everything the post mentions is 100% true and well-reasoned, especially with the inclusion of pledge/chroot/etc. for dropping privileges.

There's two diametrically opposed deployment mechanisms:

1) stack towers of glop on top of each other until you're running a simple `echo "hello world"` on top of a docker container inside a vm in a proxmox server as part of a k8s cluster under a hypervisor running on remote compute...

2) just run `bash -c 'echo "hello world"'` and front it with CGI (stateless, single binary, yada yada yada...)

Take a peek at https://github.com/Domain/bash.cgi ... not that i'm suggesting that 'bash over busybox using cgi-bin' is the "proper architecture", it's more trying to illustrate that the amount of code that holds you back from being nearly truly "frameworkless" is tiny and easy to reason about.

For some of the internal tooling I'm doing for work, I've been tending towards:

    some-cmd [--json|--markdown] ...yet-more-args...
When you use the process and shell environment itself as a repl, you start trending towards `[--cgi-bin]` would "just" be another output type, and the ability (nay: foresight!) to ensure that your commands are independent, reproducible, and only depend on their input arguments leads you directly towards being runnable in both "hostile" (ie: firecracker vm / lambda-style) or very "comfortable" environments (ie: shell, debuggers, unit/integration tests).

There are required exceptions to attorney client privilege[0]:

> the confidentiality rule is subject to limited exceptions. Paragraph (b)(1) recognizes the overriding value of life and physical integrity and permits disclosure reasonably necessary to prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm

An eventual lawyer-bot probably should be able to identify this, however this does pose a conondrum.

Top #1 — MgB2:

I really don't understand why most people here act like this is some weird unproven and unsafe technology. This is literally a solved problem. They are everywhere in Germany and it's no issue.

The inverters follow the grid AC and shut off their output if they are disconnected or unplugged, so the plug is never "hot". The power they input into your home wiring/the power grid is limited to 800 Watts as to not overload any installation. And the power meters know not to run backwards if you happen to feed power into the grid. Most can even meter how much power you fed in total (you're not going to get paid for it, though)

If you want, you can add battery storage that follows the same rules but lets you save excess power during the day to feed into your home at night or during demand spikes (washing machine, ...).

The setups are dirt cheap (often 200 - 300 EUR for an inverter and 800 - 1000 W(peak) of solar panels) and pay for themselves in about 1-3 years in saved electricity costs.

The biggest problem with plugging a generator into an outlet is you need a double ended cord. If you use everything correctly they work fine, but there are too many ways things can go wrong. The most obvious one is you plug everything in, start the generator, and the trip over the cord on you way back inside, thus sending the live male end flying toward you. Once in a while a kid will see these dual male plugs and plug them in - lots of ways things can go wrong here.

There is also the problem of backfeeding, but this is more theoretical - even if you know to limit your power use, your neighbors won't and so your generator will trip its own breaker. Linemen are taught to either treat power lines like they are live, or to short them to ground - it can happen they don't do this and you kill a linemen, but still not as big a worry as it is made out.

They make generator "inlets" that sidestep all these problems when used correctly. Most common I've seen is a block so you can't have the inlet and the main breaker both on at once.

it is not theoretical from the POV of power company employees working on their lines. the power goes out, they go to fix the equipment or wiring, and if the inverters connected to the grid have not shutdown, there could be 10s of kW to even MWs being backfed into the system they are working on.

that's why in the US at least, grid-tied inverters are required to have protection against this. if they do not see power from the grid, they shutdown (and rather quickly).

items.summary: 363 points, 396 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  363 points  ·  396 comments

Top #1 — Hendrikto:

For those who, like me, had no idea what QGIS was: It is a free Geographic Information System (GIS), which means that it deals with creating, managing, analyzing, storing, and visualizing geospatial information. Think of (3D) maps and stuff like that.

Top #2 — mootothemax:

There’s something about geospatial work that seems to break LLMs. I’ve experienced it a lot with latest versions of both Fable and Opus, and it’s the classic nightmare of confidently-spoken-but-wrong.

Yesterday, I had a relatively trivial bit of work in play using distance-weighting to measure stuff, and Claude did really well / but right at the end, despite having a success metric and lots of great results matching it, Claude insisted my maths was wrong and needed changing.

When i asked why, and pointed out that the suggested replacement would cancel out the distance-weighting entirely, it immediately agreed with me and asked to write its fifth project memory about it.

The other big ones it tends to mess up on without strict guardrails are coordinate systems; and measurements, often converting back and forth between a given nation grid and wgs84 latitude/longitude in ways that lose good amounts of precision; and then custom-coding haversine-equivalents to measure a distance that’s otherwise be a simple subtraction via the national grid coordinates. It’s baffling.

↳ reply 1 — Waterluvian:

I’ve found it to be surprisingly effective lately.

I’ve been renovating a spatial/topology validation system for an OpenLayers driven map editor for robot fleets. I set up a clean interface for spatial indexes and predicates as well as your basic geotoolbox functions.

I was most surprised by a moment where Opus detected that using a union approach to ensure that robot footprints always sat within valid polygons (possibly straddling multiple valid polygons) was slow in testing. So it decided to find the difference between footprint and each polygon within the AABB of it. And if the remaining polygon is zero size, it’s valid. If not, the remaining shape is what is invalid.

I was also surprised just how good it was at recognizing, “in the test data there’s a lot of this kind of feature so we should explore what’s more common: hits or misses?

Before robotics I spent a lot of time building spatial models for data processing and analysis. I find that I can usually just explain the spatial question in natural language and it will figure out the relevant inputs from the dataset and what the process can be. I’m not obsolete quite yet though because maybe 10-20% of the time it goes on a pretty fantastical journey through unnecessary intermediate data products.

↳↳ reply — mootothemax:

Oh don't get me wrong, it's a level-boosting monster even with that.

The worrying bit is if you're not keeping a close eye on it, very easy to think you're getting a solid system, but thanks to the internal madness it's used, your entire grid has in effect shifted 10 metres right, and any spatial measurements are far more approximate than it's letting on.

That was the bad old days for me. Nowadays I keep it locked down to specific systems for projections or actual spatial calculations, and that seems to keep it honest.

And the surprise is awesome when it happens! My favourite is all the QA steps you wish you'd had and that it reasons out on the raw data alone:

"oh hey, this one city has no data but it has a high population, oh right, that's because of this obscure lookup had a row chopped off, there you go, sorted."

I get to stand back and applaud it, honestly.

↳↳↳ reply — jasomill:

LLMs are very good at conceptually simple but tedious classification problems in general.

One that has saved me many hours: given a small subset A and a disjoint sample B of a larger set of, say, complicated JSON objects in a consistent but unknown schema, what do the objects in A have in common that isn't true of any objects in B?

Example result from Claude: The field foo contains dates between August 3 and August 7, 2016 in every record in A, and every record in B contains later dates.

Claude even correctly hypothesized that it was dealing with metadata from a document management system, that field foo was the creation date of the document, and that nearby field bar, identically 10 in all records, was the document retention period in years, and thus A represented documents that would have been purged between August 3 and August 7, 2026.

↳ reply 2 — jandrewrogers:

LLMs really don't understand space.

Top #3 — throwaway2037:

More LLM allergies.

Look at this PR: https://github.com/qgis/QGIS/pull/67731/files

The code change is so simple that Claude today could easily write this code. How will they know if an LLM wrote the code? They won't. And this policy will age like milk: Each passing month, coding LLMs are improving. It will become more difficult to "detect" an LLM-authored submission.

The best LLM policy that I have seen for an open source project is Linux. Roughly: You can use LLMs, but you are fully responsible for the code it produces. Linus acknowledges both positives and negatives to LLMs.

↳ reply 1 — dspillett:

> How will they know if an LLM wrote the code?

The problem isn't just the code - the documentation for the change explaining what it fixes, how, why, what testing has been done, and so forth is often either lacking, far to verbose, or both (massively verbose without actually containing much useful information or other sense).

You raise a valid point for the future: when the average quality of submissions is good enough that it is impossible to tell the difference between human (or human aided by AI but giving its output sufficient review/rewrite) and LLM/agent submissions, then the issue will have gone away. But, given the problems projects like this are seeing it is obvious that the technology (or the people using it, probably both) are not nearly there yet.

> The best LLM policy…

That is a great policy. If only the entire world would follow it, or in fact even ever read it.

If the only reliable way for now to not be suffocated under a mass of bad AI submissions is to refuse anything that even vaguely sniffs of AI, then that is what many projects are going to have to do. If that offends you, then fork the project and patch your changes in, or vide code one from scratch yourself, then you can keep maintaining that along with all the submissions you get for fixes. Let time tell which the right decision is :-)

↳ reply 2 — worldsavior:

LLMs are still being detected at the same level since the day coding agents were actually something, hence, it's not improving for 3 years. Why would they be undetectable next month?

Top #1 — bob1029:

SQLite + NVMe feels like cheating sometimes. If my #1 requirement is lowest possible latency, I can't imagine picking anything else.

Kestrel (AspNetCore) + SQLite + NVMe all on the same machine is where things start to get really spicy in my experience. Imagine handling an entire form submission that mutates database state in tens to low-hundreds of microseconds. Total wall clock time required to service any HTTP request can be well under a single millisecond. If your average cpu time per request is 30uS, you could approach half a million per second on a 16-32 core machine.

↳ reply 1 — Havoc:

>If my #1 requirement is lowest possible latency, I can't imagine picking anything else.

optane

↳↳ reply — globnomulous:

Intel P5800X user, checking in. The latency improvement when I switched from a Samsung 990 to the P5800X wasn't quite as mind-blowing or revelatory as the HDD to (SATA) SSD switch was ~16 years ago (OCZ Vertex LE -- $300 for 100 GB!) but compared to standard nvme it still feels like a dramatic improvement. It's startling to realize how much performance we're leaving on the table even with nvme ssds. Build times for what I work on dropped by much more than 50%, if I remember correctly, when I switched and everything on my system feels more responsive.

Edit: optane also shows what the SSD/nvme sequential-throughput marketing wars have cost us. Latency and random 4k iops always should have been the focus (in research, development, reviews, and benchmarks), not sequential throughput.

There are already 100 million HarmonyOS devices in China, so you could say it's now a three-way rivalry. The apps I use every day basically all have native HarmonyOS versions, including even foreign apps like Tesla and Sam's Club.

I've actually been using HarmonyOS for half a year now, and it feels pretty good — the notifications and system smoothness are on par with iOS. The reason I don't use an iPhone is that I need NFC access control, which iOS doesn't support.

↳ reply 1 — Someone:

It’s interesting to see how they got there. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HarmonyOS:

“From 2019 to 2024, versions 1 to 4.3 (4.5 TV) of the operating system were built by integrating the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) with OpenHarmony, allowing it to support both HarmonyOS and Android apps. The current iteration of HarmonyOS became known as HarmonyOS NEXT (later it was renamed HarmonyOS 5 in launched of Pura X). HarmonyOS NEXT was announced on August 4, 2023, and officially launched on October 22, 2024. It also replaced the OpenHarmony multi-kernel system with its own HongMeng Kernel at its core and removed all Android code. Since version 5, HarmonyOS only supports apps in its native "App" format.

HarmonyOS 5.x+ both discards the common Unix-like Linux kernel and replaces the previous multiple-kernel, kernel agnostic system from OpenHarmony with its own bespoke HarmonyOS microkernel as a single framework.”

Further fragmenting the user base into a third closed ecosystem is good because app builders have to build 3 versions so...now they'll be more willing to build a fourth version?

Top #2 — microtonal:

No, they won't become a viable alternative:

- Worse compatibility with the millions of Android apps already out there.

- Hardware vendors (outside Apple) all target Android.

- The usability of Android/iOS is far better than non-Android Linux phones.

- The security of non-Android Linux phones is in a bad state (e.g. lacking proper app sandboxing). Heck, even the Android emulation layers that some of these phones have, throw the strong Android sandbox model out of the window.

The answer is very obvious and it is AOSP. Even though Google is trying to close AOSP more (e.g. by not pushing source continuously to the AOSP Git repos and keeping QPR1/3 for themselves), it is still an open source system. Play Services can either be run sandboxed or emulated with microG. AOSP allows alternative systems to hit the ground running, you get great app compatibility, a tested security model, great usability, and support from hardware vendors, including vendors that are alternative friendly (used to be Pixel, now Motorola, Fairphone, etc.). If ever needed, AOSP could be forked and it would still be leagues ahead of non-Android Linux phones.

All the downsides that apply to AOSP-based systems (like things getting blocked by Play Integrity, unlockable bootloaders) also apply to non-Android Linux systems.

↳ reply 1 — apatheticonion:

The lack of polish is a function of the inability to use the hardware. The hardware is tightly gatekept so competition _cannot_ exist. Regulators are the only ones who can force vendors to distribute documentation for and unlock their hardware.

Once we can actually target the hardware, open source alternatives will be much better than first party options.

You can already see the potential in the open source world.

Linux has Waydroid so Android apps can be run on Linux at full speed without emulation. That means, if you had a Linux phone, you have the entire Android library - the only thing lacking is the launcher. How hard is a launcher to program? It's just Steam's big picture mode.

Other examples of the nice things we can't have; FEX lets you run Steam games on phone hardware. Open source drivers can unlock displayport over USBC. Instantly your phone becomes a thin client / laptop replacement that can play PC games (poorly, but 1080p games are possible).

We are _not allowed_ to do these things. I love OS development and, if I was allowed, I'd make iOS look like janky trash.

↳↳ reply — microtonal:

But they publish device trees, driver sources, and firmware. Most AOSP-based projects support Fairphone, as well as PostmarketOS and ubports.

The problem is not only hardware support, the problem is also that the stack on top of it is very immature compared to AOSP and not something you could give to a daily phone user.

It’s funny that you mention Waydroid. It throws most of Android’s strong security model out of the window.

↳↳↳ reply — apatheticonion:

> So, where are the super-polished Linux systems for the Fairphone?

It still has tiny market reach. Very few people are going to invest the time needed to build a quality user experience for like 1000 users.

Just imagine what would happen if Linux could be installed on the iPhone. There would be SteamOS distributions within an hour of the announcement.

> It’s funny that you mention Waydroid. It throws most of Android’s strong security model out of the window.

Haha yea, it's more an example of capabilities that could be rolled into highly polished user experiences. Again, if Linux could be installed on the iPhone - I'm certain Waydroid maintainers would shut the project down from PRs.

~~* competition *~~

↳ reply 2 — opengears:

Yes, the Librem 5 is a bit older phone with some rough edges, but for me it is a really good phone. It gives freedom in the free software sense, and consistency with my Linux computers. I gladly accept some minor inconvenience to have a phone that respects my freedom and privacy.

I cannot foresee the future, but for me the experience on a Linux phone that I control is far more superior than any phone that spies on me and takes away my freedom, like Android or iOS, basically any phone from any manufacturer that disrespects me.

items.title: Whatever became of holography? (2011)
items.summary: 163 points, 95 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (americanscientist.org)

→ HN comments  ·  163 points  ·  95 comments

Top #1 — adastra22:

Very few people in the comments seem to understand what holography is. A hologram is not a “3D display” that mimics a sci-fi movie or TV show. A hologram is photographic media / display technology that records and transmits phase as well as intensity of incident photons. By capturing all the properties of the electromagnetic field that strikes the film, and re-emitting the same EM wave when stimulated, the hologram ends up being a full “3D picture” because after all, the light that hits your eyes ends up being the same as if you were looking at the actual scene. But that’s a consequence, not the defining property.

3blue1brown has a great explainer video on what holograms are: https://youtu.be/EmKQsSDlaa4

↳ reply 1 — dTal:

Well, yes, but actually, no...

"Hologram" is one of those words that has a wide variety of overlapping meanings. You can be a strict prescriptionist about it and insist that a real hologram involves laser light, interference patterns, 3D scene replication, phase preservation etc, but there will always be something that doesn't quite meet your definition that nevertheless is called a "hologram" by large numbers of people, even expert optical scientists:

A digital holographic stereogram prints an array of hogels (holographic pixels); the hogels themselves are holograms, but are mutually incoherent across the plate. When implemented to the highest level, the result is perceptually and behaviorally indistinguishable from an analog hologram.

A rainbow hologram (such as are found on credit cards) has single parallax only - it certainly does not capture all the properties of any particular electromagnetic field. No purity here, it's just a nifty tech for making things look 3D that happens to exploit wave interference. And everyone calls those holograms.

A scratch hologram is, to a first approximation, an extremely coarse version of a rainbow hologram, made by hand by engraving curved grooves in a reflective material. Now we're away from lasers and wave interference, and for this we sacrifice color - but geometrically we are still dealing with directional microreflections on a surface. Hologram? Depends who you ask.

Lenticular holograms use refraction rather than diffraction to achieve essentially the same imaging model as a rainbow hologram, but in a decidedly less finicky way, at the expense of some resolution. The same imaging data could be used to make a lenticular or a rainbow hologram. No lasers, no diffraction. Hologram? Depends who you ask...

My advice, as someone who has worked with holograms for a decade, is to give up. Saying "AKTUALLY Tupac/Abba isn't a hologram" gets old after the 1000th time. In the real world, "hologram" means "intangible optical simulacra", regardless of how it was achieved. If you want more precision than that, you have to specify the actual technology - Denisyuk, rainbow, lenticular, etc...

When someone asks "can you make a hologram of this", you don't lecture them on optical physics. You say "sure, you want the expensive kind or the plastic kind?"

↳↳ reply — mhalle:

Having also spent a long time in actual holography, I would agree with your assessment generally and your catalog of different "holographic" techniques.

I might quibble with lenticular displays, since they have a name that predates holography.

In the ideal world, a larger umbrella term would have emerged. "Autostereoscopic" describes any display that provides different views without glasses, but that typically suggests discrete views.

"Plenogram" would have been reasonable following Adelson and Bergen's plenoptic function, but that didn't and won't happen.

"Hologram" now basically means a sufficiently advanced three-dimensional display in popular culture. And that even leaves of other real holograms, such as the ones used for non-destructive testing.

↳↳↳ reply — Melatonic:

Do these all actually only capture and display in stereo ?

↳ reply 2 — margalabargala:

I don't understand the distinction. You said it's not a 3d display, then described a 3d display technology.

That's like saying a CRT doesn't display a picture because it energizes pixels only one at a time.

↳ reply 3 — PaulHoule:

Speckle tends to make holograms look awful.

Holograms compete with many other display technologies such as stereograms, VR headsets, as well as volumetric and light field displays. This technology is described as "holographic"

https://lookingglassfactory.com/

but it looks better than holograms because it uses incoherent light field technology that doesn't have the speckle, plus the pipeline to make content for it doesn't require lasers, special equipment or special skills.

Top #2 — ubj:

Dan Smalley's research lab at BYU is actively developing 3D volumetric holography technology.

https://youtu.be/N12i_FaHvOU

The video is a bit old, but it has a few fun demos of the capabilities they've developed.

↳ reply 1 — mojuba:

Strictly speaking that's not holography if I understood it correctly. Holography is based on interference created by a surface with a special pattern, and it doesn't require any matter other than the diffractive surface. Whereas here they say they move "particles" (what particles? dust? atoms?). Still pretty cool of course and a thing on its own.

items.title: Fingerprints are the new cookies
items.summary: 286 points, 134 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (royfish.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  286 points  ·  134 comments

Top #1 — legitster:

Every time this resurfaces I like to remind people that this is mostly impractical and not how things actually work at the commercial level.

Just because someone can theoretically demonstrate your fingerprint today doesn't mean you have the same fingerprint in a few days. It's that kind of stability that you actually need for consistent matching for advertising or tracking purposes.

90% of commercial fingerprinting services still rely mostly on the IP address. Once you remove the IP address, you're left with a set of configurations that have a very short half life - volume settings, installed fonts, software versions, etc. You can expect a good portion of your audience to degrade within a couple of days. (Whereas a cookie has a life of 2 years - practically though they only survive a few months).

What you actually pay for from third party vendors is a connection made around a more stable data point - a phone number, an email address, a user ID, etc. With one of these data points you can actually track people across multiple devices for as long as you want.

items.title: Passkeys are a trap
items.summary: 515 points, 287 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (nonfunctional.substack.com)

→ HN comments  ·  515 points  ·  287 comments

Top #1 — agwa:

Note that attestation can only be required during credential registration; at login time it's not possible to retroactively require attestation if it wasn't obtained during registration. And browsers will throw up a permission prompt if a website requests attestation. Are Netflix and Twitter currently requesting attestation when people register passkeys, and rejecting the registration if the user declines the permission prompt? I very much doubt it, since Apple's passkey implementation doesn't support attestation.

Therefore, the author's scenario that sites will wait until most of their users are using attested passkeys and then "flip the switch and start rejecting non-attested passkeys" isn't very plausible.

Attestation is certainly a stain on the WebAuthn spec, and it would have been better if Chrome and Firefox didn't support attestation (unless perhaps the browser is enrolled in enterprise management), but this blog post is presenting a hypothetical and unlikely scenario. That's not a good enough reason to recommend TOTP instead, given that TOTP is vulnerable to phishing and passkeys aren't.

If consumer-facing sites start requesting attestation when registering passkeys, they deserve to be vigorously called out, and maybe then the recommendation to use passkeys should be revisited. But until that happens, don't tell people not to use passkeys.

↳ reply 1 — throwawayffffas:

> at login time it's not possible to retroactively require attestation if it wasn't obtained during registration.

Of course it is, the site will reject the passkey and require you to create one that is attested.

> Are Netflix and Twitter currently requesting attestation when people register passkeys, and rejecting the registration if the user declines the permission prompt?

They could start tomorrow.

> a hypothetical and unlikely scenario.

You have not been paying attention, that scenario is where this whole thing is building towards.

> If consumer-facing sites start requesting attestation when registering passkeys, they deserve to be vigorously called out

It's going to be the banks first.

Why called out, it's all for your safety, to make sure you are not using an insecure client that might leak your data.

↳↳ reply — lxgr:

> They could start tomorrow.

They could also start requiring you to mail a DNA sample to create an account tomorrow.

> It's going to be the banks first.

The same banks that (in the US) largely don’t even systematically use 2FA for online banking logins and completely ignore 3DS for card payments?

Attestation usually requires customers to buy and carry extra hardware, so I highly doubt it.

↳ reply 2 — WorldMaker:

Also worth point out that Apple consumer devices intentionally do not support attestation at all, and only support it for devices under enterprise management. That's still a dominant enough number of devices in the US at least that a consumer site seems unlikely to want to disable/break logins for all iOS and iPadOS users.

↳ reply 3 — xg15:

Sorry, bit this is just the standard "boil the frog" playbook that tech companies always use for user-hostile features. It's usually:

1) There is this new entirely optional feature, but it's not relevant to you, so feel free to ignore it.

2) The feature is now active by default, but no worries, there is a simple button for you to opt-out.

3) The feature is active by default, but because we value our users, there is an option in the advanced settings to deactivate it.

4) Our data shows that 99.9% of users activated the feature, but if you belong to the handful of diehards who still refuse to use it (rolls eyes), you can use this obscure command line flag or about:config entry to turn it off

5) Managing opt-out infrastructure for the feature has significant maintenance and security cost that we feel, we can no longer justify. Therefore, effective in three months, the opt-out flags will stop working and the feature will become mandatory. According to our metrics, this will affect 0.0001% of our users, so no disruption is expected.

Top #2 — bmitch3020:

I've yet to voluntarily enable passkeys, for the main reason that I want portability, and not to be tied to any single device that can be lost. I want to be able to backup and lock my credentials in a safe. I also want to control the strength of my credentials for different services, and I don't consider my thumbprint used to unlock my phone to be as strong as a long password in a password manager.

The first time I was forced to use a passkey implemented within the vendor's app (3rd party password managers were not an option). I quickly closed that account.

The second time was an app that popped up a passkey opt-in in the middle of a bunch of transaction screens. I quickly realized the error, but there was no easy undo. The opt in was one green button in the middle of the screen. Turning it back off required digging through settings to find the security option to disable, and then confirm my choice multiple times. That process also signed out all my other devices.

The fact that companies are resorting to dark patterns and forced requirements, where my money is held hostage, should be pretty good evidence of how poorly the passkey rollout is going.

↳ reply 1 — BadBadJellyBean:

You can put your passkey in another safe. I store mine in my vaultwarden. You can also do keepass with a plugin. You don't have to store it on your phone.

↳↳ reply — crote:

There is no truly secure options for this, unfortunately. Passkeys have to be online to enroll additional keys, so any kind of software or smartphone solution is going to depend completely on cloud sync. Any form of offline copy stored in a physical safe will quickly be outdated.

It gets even worse when you want to have separate passkeys, so that you have the possibility of knowing which one was compromised and doing a partial revocation: the cloud sync now requires every device to have access to every copy, so that you can individually enroll them during registration.

Yubikey of course suffers most from this, as their hardware tokens are physically incapable of any kind of sync, so a Yubikey passkey is very quickly a single-point-of-failure. They proposed[0] a system which would allow enrolling a "backup key" (which could then be safely locked in a vault, far away from day-to-day use), but with the various Big Tech companies pushing their own proprietary cloud-synced passkey implementations that of obviously went nowhere.

[0]: https://www.yubico.com/blog/yubico-proposes-webauthn-protoco...

↳↳↳ reply — WorldMaker:

Most website implementations that support passkeys have to support multiple key enrollment. It's the only long-term reliable way for the many, many users that are cross-ecosystem, which especially means Windows users in the age of no Windows Phone. Every Windows user has either an Android or iPhone. You can bootstrap with Bluetooth LTE access to your phone for a Passkey, but it's a rough web experience if the user needs to do that every time they access a page, so most good flows ask the user the enroll a Windows PC passkey in addition to their phone's passkey and really good ones make use of a passkey auto-enrollment option designed for this scenario (Bluetooth passkey to "local" passkey auto-enrollment).

Perhaps surprisingly, Windows has helped keep Passkeys from being "proprietary" lock-in because Microsoft no longer has users in a single ecosystem.

There is no dedicated auto-enrollment for "backup" keys, but most consumer sites make it very easy to enroll "backup" keys yourself.

Also, Passkeys don't have to be "online" to enroll additional keys. Each key is independent, enrolling is just generating new keys. The trouble is that web browsers generate lots of Passkeys (at least one per domain, at the very least) so if you in theory want to print them all and store them in a physical vault it might be a hefty book you are printing.

Cloud sync isn't required. Most users want it so that they don't have a single-point-of-failure.

As an implementation detail some Passkeys have a master key that is then used in some key derivation function (KDF) to generate the hundreds or thousands of individual passkeys (at least one per domain), and that's what most Yubikey passkey implementations need to do because Yubikeys weren't designed to store lots of keys, so it is devices like Yubikey that makes it seem like Passkeys are less independent than they really are.

↳ reply 2 — freakynit:

Same for me.. I don't want my login information to be tied to a particular device, or device vendor. TOTP is a clear winner in all of this. Minor inconvenience, but highly secure and portable.

Top #3 — danpalmer:

The very last thing, past the conclusion, the very last footnote is:

> Addendum: I feel I have made a compelling case for passkeys in this article. And I haven’t even pointed out one of their best security features: they are (in most use cases) domain-bound, meaning they are resistant to what are called Man-In-The-Middle attacks.

"I made a compelling case... but didn't point out the most important security feature that motivated passkeys in the first place"

Honestly I don't think this post did make a compelling case. There's a lot of assuming bad faith on the part of the FIDO alliance, while completely missing that preventing MITM attacks was a key design feature. The FIDO alliance members deal with stolen accounts all the time, and passkeys largely solve that. Stealing accounts is almost always done with phishing or social engineering, and passkeys solve the former and reduce the surface for the latter.

↳ reply 1 — kevin_nisbet:

I sort of started skimming when the article was saying industry solved the problem with text messages and TOTP. I think there are several arguable problems with Passkeys as implemented, but to argue TOTP is equivalent is going to leave lots of people vulnerable.

The protections against MITM you mentioned is probably the biggest one, but the other one in the back of my mind is TOTP is a shared secret. So a compromise of the server side allows impersonation of users undetected, which can be a big problem. Maybe I'm over reacting because no company has ever lost a copy of it's database and they're all super secure. But, imagine trying to argue as a user I didn't do a thing when there is an audit log saying we challenged the user for TOTP and it was provided, was definitely the users fault.

↳↳ reply — danpalmer:

TOTP is this decade's "just have a better password", and we all know how well that went before.

↳↳↳ reply — yread:

I think it's rather this millenium's "just check the domain really carefully". You can't choose a weak TOTP, write it on a post it or share TOTPs on multiple websites. The main (only?) failure mode is that you type it in an attacker-controlled input.

↳ reply 2 — MBCook:

It’s not just man in the middle.

If the credentials get stolen from a website database, they’re useless for every other website on earth. No matter how poorly they’re stored, it’s just a public key and is not useful. Hell, they can get code executing on the webserver that collects full login information, and it’s not useful.

Passwords always require full transmission. Hashing for storage requires a proper implementation, which we’ve seen does not happen. 100% of the time. There’s a reason hackers are still stealing passwords from websites after three decades.

Passkeys solve that. Nothing else available to the average user does.

Top #2 — plaidfuji:

I generally agree with the prevailing commentary here, i.e. that automating app development and maths proofs may not be as world-changing as the Artificial Intelligentsia purport / “fear” it to be.

But also, upon more reflection, it occurred to me that if we’re able to create a competent humanoid robot, that could legitimately be world changing in some good and other very bad ways. The scary part is that I don’t believe there’s any major physical / energetic barrier to this. The hardware exists, the power supplies are light enough. The only part that’s lagging is the software and motion contols; the intelligence. The part that is experiencing breakthroughs at an accelerating pace.

What if a highly intelligent and physically competent robot were available for the price of a cheap car, say ~$20k? What if that robot were competent enough to cook, clean, assist the elderly, move things around, assemble and disassemble things, etc? Billions of jobs would be displaced, or hit with a very concrete maximum wage.

Many white collar jobs, while still at risk for displacement as well, benefit from barriers like IT integration and data privacy hurdles, and the fact that corporate higher-ups simply prefer to communicate with humans.

But most blue collar / manual labor jobs have almost the opposite condition: humans introduce risk, and generally don’t enhance anybody’s “experience” - see people’s somewhat odd acceptance of higher fares for a Waymo vs an Uber. [1]

I don’t think we’re there yet, but the fact that we are rapidly accelerating our trajectory toward that world should be at the least, unsettling.

[1] https://techcrunch.com/2025/06/12/waymo-rides-cost-more-than...

Top #1 — GMoromisato:

I've more or less followed this advice, and it's worked out for me. For the most part, I used my salary to pay for expenses and stock compensation to build up wealth.

The tricky part is that a lot of this advice is situation-dependent. Should you switch to a riskier company that offers a higher compensation? Sometimes yes, sometimes no. Should you work late to accomplish goals hoping to get a promotion? It depends.

So how are we supposed to know what to do?

The answer, in my opinion, is people. You have to trust people who are trustworthy and avoid people who are not. As an employee, your success depends on the people who hired you--they are the ones who can promote you or cheat you. The best leaders are the ones who realize that helping you advance is going to help them advance. Help your boss accomplish their corporate goals and they will promote you--not as a reward, but as a bet that you will help them on the next goal.

Bad leaders are either too selfish (fail to promote you) or too incompetent (unable to rise, even with your help). You need to learn to avoid them.

Therefore, my advice is this: Look at the leaders in your company--people who could plausibly hire you. Which ones are the best bets? Which ones have both the talent and the integrity to succeed? If you're lucky there's more than one and you can work to get on their team. If you're unlucky, there are none and you need to find a different company.

Top #3 — tripletao:

The bad cancer example is interesting to the extent it reveals that one of the world's top mathematicians is apparently unaware that applied science runs almost entirely on half-understood semi-empirical methods. That's most true for medicine, given the extreme complexity of human life; but if you look at a modern SPICE model for a transistor, a device that we claim to understand at the level of subatomic particles, then you'll find it's full of curve fits. As an engineer, I find that perfectly normal. My job is to use all the tools at my disposal to meet some human desire (to not die of exposure, for a slightly thinner phone, etc.), and whatever fundamental understanding I might have is only one tool to that end.

My impression is that since pure mathematics doesn't attempt to meet those human desires they need some other objective, and that objective is human understanding. The loss of that is thus felt more heavily than in other fields. We could say it's their problem, and they need to get over it just like the chess players did; but the outside implications are broader here, since mathematicians working in fields they themselves considered useless have so frequently been wrong--in Hardy's Mathematician's Apology, he gave number theory as an example of such a field, unaware of what the cryptographers would achieve just decades later.

It's possible that AI-generated pure math will continue this trend of delivering extraordinary unexpected societal value. It's also possible that the humans won't ever sufficiently understand that math, and the machines won't ever sufficiently understand human desires, and that connection won't be made. I've never met a pure mathematician who considered those downstream applications to be an important contributor to their motivations; but as AI-generated math contributes to the argument to allocate a large and increasing share of GDP to datacenter buildouts, that question of whether downstream value requires human understanding seems pressing.

items.summary: 204 points, 140 comments. See description for top comments.
items.html:
→ Article (disconnect3d.pl)

→ HN comments  ·  204 points  ·  140 comments

Top #1 — amarshall:

Or you can just…not quote the tilde. Folks always seem to reflexively quote “strings” in Bash while not realizing that (almost) everything is a string and most strings are not quoted and it would be odd to do it (e.g. no one is doing `"ls" "-a" "foo"`).

↳ reply 1 — kragen:

Not quoting the tilde doesn't help:

    : tmp; echo $PATH:~
    /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games:~
Edit: mjmas points out that I am wrong, because different Calvinball rules apply to variable assignments:

    : tmp; x=$PATH:~
    : tmp; echo "$x"
    /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games:/home/user
Also in general your advice is very bad advice. In command-line arguments, which is the vast majority of the code of any shell script, you should always quote strings that contain variable expansion unless you want them to be implicitly split on spaces after variable expansion, because the thing you're storing in the variable is not an atomic string but rather a space-separated list.

This is almost never what you actually want, and in the rare cases that you do want to store a list, the shell's implicit space splitting usually breaks on filenames containing spaces. Bash has actual array variables which make it possible, but horrible, to handle this in a first-class way:

    : tmp; x=("foo bar" baz)
    : tmp; echo "${x[@]}"
    foo bar baz
    : tmp; touch "${x[@]}"
    : tmp; ls -l "${x[@]}"
    -rw-r--r-- 1 user user 0 Oct 11 17:52  baz
    -rw-r--r-- 1 user user 0 Oct 11 17:52 'foo bar'
This ksh feature is absent in the Bourne shell and in dash, but MirBSD ksh, Bash, and zsh all have it.

In general, whenever you see a $variable $expansion in a shell script outside of double quotes, you should suspect that the shell script will probably fail if your filenames or directory names contain spaces. In very many cases, this results in path injection security vulnerabilities. There are contexts where unquoted $variable $expansion is safe, but they are relatively rare.

However, relevant detail here! One of those safe contexts is actually variable assignment, where as mjmas pointed out in their helpful comment below, unquoted variable expansion is actually perfectly safe:

    : tmp; a='x  y'
    : tmp; b=α:$a:ω
    : tmp; echo "$b"
    α:x  y:ω
